Nutribus 2.0 activity and inclusive impact dashboard guide

Overview of system objectives, field tracking scope, and interactive navigation controls

What This Is

The centralized monitoring platform tracking the Nutribus 2.0 campaign. It brings together field data from 64 primary schools and 640 community cooking demonstrations (10 demonstrations in the community around each school) across all 9 Karamoja districts (Abim, Amudat, Kaabong, Karenga, Kotido, Moroto, Nabilatuk, Nakapiripirit, and Napak).

What It Is Used For

It monitors real-time headcounts, inclusive reach for learners and adults with disabilities (PWDs), and verified adoption across Nutrition, Education, and Gender: tracking teacher/VHT orientations, 3-visit school contact cycles, community cooking demonstrations, Metu porridge local fortification, gender chore rebalancing, and firewood-saving cookstoves.

How to Navigate It

Filter Bar (Above): Select any district, adjust the start/end date range, or type keywords in the search bar to reactively update all metrics and tables. Click Reset Filters anytime.
Activity Tabs (Below): Switch across the 7 activity tabs to explore specific activity reports, qualitative Change Stories, and field monitoring results.

(2) What specific action are you personally going to take this week? (3) Record their Specific personal action in their exact words. (4) Sex.

Quality Checks

Facilitation quality, inclusive participation and comprehension

Field coordinator quality assurance checklist recorded during activation:

Did learners actively handle materials and practice rather than listen passively? Yes: 100% (63/63 Schools)
Did all three age bands and both boys and girls participate? Yes: 100% (63/63 Schools)
Was any learner excluded or left out during sessions? No: 100% (63/63 Schools)
Zero learners excluded; active buddy system supported learners with disabilities.
Were materials understood without long/confusing explanation? Yes: 100% (63/63 Schools)
Why: Visual flashcards, color-coded food grouping cards, and hands-on Metu porridge demonstrations allowed immediate comprehension without complex explanations across Ngakarimojong dialects.
Pillar 3: Community & Clean Cooking Barrier Diagnostic

Primary reasons for low uptake or preparation know-how of WFP's Metu porridge

Diagnostic evaluating why households struggle with Metu porridge preparation despite cash support or market access

Key Diagnostic Finding:

Across 63 reporting schools, 45 schools cite ingredients not prioritized at household level, alongside 23 citing taste preferences, 15 citing recipe confidence/skills, and 24 citing limited access to cooking materials. Practical cooking demos directly address these prioritization and preparation barriers.

Pillar 2: Rebalancing chores and attendance (33,812 boy responses recorded)

Read out the following statements and count number who agree. Aggregated across all participating schools with verbatim boy reflections:

Consensus: 94.7% Average Agreement (32,021 / 33,812)
Statement 1 5773 / 6990 Agreed (82.6)
It is unfair for a girl to stay home doing compound work while brothers leave early for class.
Reason in their words:

"Nakapiripirit: "The girl may not concentrate like aboy""

Statement 2 6885 / 7026 Agreed (98.0)
Boys and girls should finish morning chores at the same time so both eat porridge and walk to school together.
Reason in their words:

"Nakapiripirit: "To make work easy""

Statement 3 6237 / 6382 Agreed (97.7)
Collecting firewood for cooking is a chore that boys and girls should do together.
Reason in their words:

"Nakapiripirit: "To offer campany to and security to girls from rapiest""

Statement 4 6693 / 6812 Agreed (98.3)
I am ready to fetch water from borehole in morning so my sister is not late/punished.
Reason in their words:

"Nakapiripirit: "Share work with my sister""

Statement 5 6433 / 6602 Agreed (97.4)
If a girl misses school to herd animals or do chores I will speak up to get her back to class.
Reason in their words:

"Nakapiripirit: "Girls are not to look after animas while boys go to school""

Qualitative field observations and written school commitments

Key delivery issues, key successes, adaptations for next school, and exact written school commitments recorded by field teams:

Kaabong West Primary School Kaabong
Key delivery issue or barrier observed:

"High ambient wind created sound distortion during outdoor cooking demo microphone setup."

Key success observed:

"Over 180 boys joined the water jerrican balancing relay and loudly pledged to share water-fetching chores."

One adaptation to make before next school:

"Shift subsequent demo circle into the lee side of the main classroom block to shield against wind noise."

Written School Commitment in exact words:
"We the teachers and pupils of Kaabong West commit that every child will receive porridge with greens, and boys will fetch morning water so girls never arrive late."
Lomorunyankori Primary School Moroto
Key delivery issue or barrier observed:

"Dusty wind made paper flashcards vulnerable to tearing during peer group food sorting."

Key success observed:

"Headteacher pledged school woodlot trees for shade-based NutriClub demonstrations and SMC provided clean storage."

One adaptation to make before next school:

"Laminate all visual demo charts and mount them on weighted wooden tripods."

Written School Commitment in exact words:
"Lomorunyankori P/S commits to establish an active NutriClub meeting every Wednesday and supporting female attendance through chore rebalancing."
Acegeretolim Primary School Nabilatuk
Key delivery issue or barrier observed:

"Local dialect differences in scientific nutrition terms required prompt translation into Ngakarimojong."

Key success observed:

"Community elders who attended stayed for the full chore dialogue and agreed with boys' public pledges."

One adaptation to make before next school:

"Engage lead local language teacher as co-facilitator alongside WFP NutriBus coordinator."

Written School Commitment in exact words:
"Acegeretolim school management and parents commit to monitor morning girl-child attendance and enforce equal chore allocation at household kraals."

Pillar What was done (Numbers) How well it was done (Quality) What changed in daily life
Pillar 1: School feeding.
School Meal Protection & METU-1
Fortification Mastery: 48.9% Fortification recall pass
16 Orientations · 65 Visit 1 · 63 Visit 2 · 13 Visit 3 Closeouts Logged
  • • Protect school meal & learning: 16 primary schools completed orientation with 1522 stakeholders logged across activities
  • • Promote balanced plate & METU-1 porridge: Anchor multi-mix recipe using locally available greens (Eboo, Lokaka) and cowpeas (63 schools delivered Visit 2 reaching 79,102 learners)
  • • Strengthen nutrition clubs & gardens: 58 active clubs (2528 registered members across active schools); demo gardens, OFSP & iron-rich beans tracked
  • • Raise awareness of WFP helpline (0800 210 210): Toll-free reporting promoted for theft or mismanagement of school meals
 Unaided Fortification Recall
  • • Unaided recall of METU-1 fortification ingredients across activation schools
  • • 351 of 438 village demos (80.1%) strictly sourced seasonal local foods
  • • WFP helpline (0800 210 210) display boards handed over across all schools
 Protected Meals & Fortification
  • • 159 of 226 Home NutriCharts returned (70.4%) with 128 joint completions across 13 Visit 3 schools
  • • 438 of 640 community demonstration reports recorded (317 demonstrating Metu porridge fortification)
  • • 73 of 78 Visit 3 household interviews confirmed youngest child served first (93.6%)
Pillar 2: Gender.
Fair Sharing & Allyship
Boy Allyship Consensus: 94.7% (33,812 boy responses)
58 NutriClubs · 65 Visit 1 · 63 Visit 2 · 13 Visit 3 Closeouts Logged
  • • Fair sharing at table & classroom: Parity audited across 65 schools (49,997 boys, 43,089 girls)
  • • Structured dialogues with allies: Boys, fathers & male teachers engaged as allies (33,812 boy responses, 94.7% agreement)
  • • Address practical constraints: Tackling domestic labour (water & firewood chores), cost, and menstruation to keep girls in class
  • • Target: 64 primary schools across 3-visit longitudinal cycles
 Consensus on Chore Rebalancing
  • • Micro-polls affirm domestic chores should be shared equally
  • • 20,151 attendees recorded across 207 active NutriClub sessions (9031 girls, 11120 boys)
  • • Inclusive accommodation verified (21577 PWD attendees across sessions)
 Chore Rebalancing Committed
  • • Polled consensus on boys fetching water (94.7%) & 68 of 78 Visit 3 interviews confirmed morning chore shifts (87.2%)
  • • Longitudinal attendance tracked across Visit 1 (93,301), Visit 2 (79,102), and Visit 3 (13,675 weekly pupils)
  • • 100% (11 of 13) of Visit 3 audited schools confirmed active chronic absentee tracing
Pillar 3: Community engagement.
640 Demos & Clean Cooking
Joint Action Calendars: 81.2% (13 of 16 schools)
438 Cooking Demos · 13 Joint Calendars Agreed · 62 Patrons Appointed
  • • 640 Cooking Demonstrations target: 438 demonstrations logged to date led by VHT/lead-mother pairs (233 sessions with lead mothers)
  • • Community dialogues with men & elders: 440 male community members engaged in Visit 2; 13 of 16 schools agreed on 4-week joint calendars
  • • Clean & smart cooking practices: Fuelwood pre-drying, pot covering, retained heat cooking, moving from 3-stone fires
  • • METU-1 recipe chart routine: 1,835 take-home NutriCharts issued for household routine adoption
 18.8% Multi-Partner Engagement
  • • District Education Offices, Health Centres, UNAC & AFI co-facilitated across sessions
  • • 230 of 438 community demos (52.5%) featured hands-on caregiver cooking practice
  • • 362 of 438 village demos (82.6%) demonstrated clean/smart cooking practices
 Clean Cooking & Recipe Adoption
  • • 12 of 13 Visit 3 schools honored commitments & 12 of 13 verified improved fuel-saving kitchen stoves
  • • 362 of 438 community demos demonstrated fuelwood conservation, pot covering & improved stoves
  • • 415 of 438 village demos (94.7%) executed structured community gender & consensus dialogues
